question.text:
Consider set $A = \{1,2,3,4,5\}.$ From all the subsets of $A,$ we define a new set $X$ as
$X = \{(P,Q) \mid |P \Delta Q| = 2\},$
where $(P,Q)$ is ordered pair $(P,Q)$ and $\Delta$ denotes the symmetric difference operation.
The number of elements in $X,$ i.e., $|X|$ is $\_\_\_\_\_$

Consider a propositional language where

  • $p$ means "Bonny is happy",
  • $q$ means "Bonny plays a music",
  • $r$ means "Seema is happy".

The propositional formula for the sentence:

"if Bonny is happy and plays a music then Seema isn’t happy" is?

(Mark all the appropriate choices)

  1. $p \wedge q \rightarrow \neg r$
  2. $p \vee q \rightarrow \neg r$
  3. $\neg p \vee \neg q \vee \neg r$
  4. $p \vee q \rightarrow  r$

Two finite sets $X$ and $Y$ have $m$ and $n$ elements each. The number of subsets of $X$ is $96$ more than that of $Y.$ The values of $m,n$ respectively are
  1. $4,7$
  2. $7,4$
  3. $5,7$
  4. $7,5$

Which of the following is the correct formalization for the sentence
"No student loves Bill"? 

(Mark all the appropriate choices)

  1. $\neg \exists x(\text{Student}(x) \wedge \text{Loves}(x,Bill))$
  2. $\forall x(\neg \text{Student}(x) \vee \neg \text{Loves}(x,Bill))$
  3. $\forall x(\neg \text{Student}(x) \vee \text{Loves}(x,Bill))$
  4. $\forall x(\neg \text{Student}(x) \wedge \neg \text{Loves}(x,Bill))$

Let $f$ be a function from set $A$ to set $B.$ Let $S$ and $T$ be two subsets of $A.$ Now, consider the statements given below.

  • $S_1:$ $f(S \cup T ) = f (S) \cup f (T ).$
  • $S_2:$ $f(S \cap T ) = f (S) \cap f (T ).$

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

  1. Only $S_1$ is true
  2. Only $S_2$ is true
  3. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are true
  4. Neither $S_1$ nor $S_2$ is true

If $R$ and $S$ are two equivalence relations on a set $A,$ then which of the below statements is/are TRUE?

  • $S_1: R \cup S$ is an equivalence relation.
  • $S_2: R \cap S$ is an equivalence relation.
  1. $S_1$ is true and $S_2$ is false
  2. $S_1$ is false and $S_2$ is true
  3. Neither $S_1$ nor $S_2$ is true
  4. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are true

Consider the following two identities on three sets $X,Y$ and $Z.$ (Here $\Delta$ represents the symmetric difference operation)

  • $S_1: X - (Y \cup Z) = (X-Y) \cap (X-Z)$
  • $S_2: X \Delta(Y \cap Z) = (X \Delta Y) \cap (X \Delta Z)$

Which of the following options is TRUE?

  1. Only $S_1$ is True
  2. Only $S_2$ is True
  3. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are True
  4. Neither $S_1$ nor $S_2$ is True

Define a relation $P$ on the set of all functions from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ as
$fPg$ if and only if there is a $k \in \mathbb{R} $ such that $f(x) = g(x)$ for every $x\geq k$. Which of the following is TRUE?
  1. $P$ is reflexive as well as symmetric
  2. $P$ is not reflexive
  3. $P$ is not Transitive
  4. $P$ is not Symmetric

Consider the following two sentences

  • $S_1:$ The intersection of two transitive relations is transitive.
  • $S_2:$ The union of two transitive relations is transitive.

Which of the below options is/are CORRECT?

  1. Only $S_1$
  2. Only $S_2$
  3. Neither $S_1$ nor $S_2$
  4. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$

Which of the following is correct formalization of the sentence

"There is a student who is loved by every other student."?

Here, $\text{Loves}(p,q)$ means $p \text{ loves } q.$

  1. $\exists x(\text{Student}(x) \wedge \forall y(\text{Student}(y) \rightarrow \text{Loves}(y,x)))$
  2. $\exists x(\text{Student}(x) \wedge \forall y(\text{Student}(y) \wedge \neg(y=x) \rightarrow \text{Loves}(y,x)))$
  3. $\exists x(\text{Student}(x) \rightarrow \forall y(\text{Student}(y) \wedge \text{Loves}(y,x)))$
  4. $\exists x(\text{Student}(x) \rightarrow \forall y(\text{Student}(y) \wedge \neg(y=x) \wedge \text{Loves}(y,x)))$

Suppose that $h:\mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ is known to be one-one and onto (bijection). Let's define a function $f:\mathbb{Z}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ by $f(x,y)=h(x)+h(y).$ Which of the following defines the nature of function $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f$ is one-one
  2. $f$ is onto
  3. $f$ is a bijection
  4. $f$ is neither one-one nor onto

Which of the following is the negation of the statement
"All pentagon are polygon".

  1. All pentagon are not polygon
  2. There is some pentagon which is not polygon
  3. All polygons are pentagon
  4. There is some pentagon which is polygon

For every athlete $A,$ if $A$ is successful then $A$ has good skills and $A$ is hardworking.
Which one of the following sentences is equivalent to the above claim.

  1. For every athlete $A$, if $A$ does not have good skills or $A$ is not hardworking, then $A$ is not successful
  2. There is an athlete $A,$ such that if $A$ does not have good skills or $A$ is not hardworking, then $A$ is not successful
  3. If $A$ does not have good skills or $A$ is not hardworking, then $A$ is not successful
  4. None of these

Consider three finite sets $A, B$ and $C.$ Let $S_1 = ((A \cap B) - (B \cap C)) - C$ and $S_2 = (A - (A - C)) - (A -B)$. The sets $S_1$ and $S_2$ are related as.
  1. $S_1 \subset S_2$
  2. $S_1 \supset S_2$
  3. $S_1 = S_2$
  4. None of these

Consider the following statements assuming there is at least one tomato, one fruit and one vegetable:

  • $S_1:$ All tomatoes are vegetables. All fruits are vegetables. Therefore, some tomatoes are fruits.
  • $S_2:$ Some tomatoes are fruits. All fruits are vegetables. Therefore, some tomatoes are vegetables.

Which of the following options is correct about the above statements?

  1. $S_1$ is correct but $S_2$ is not correct
  2. $S_1$ is not correct but $S_2$ is correct
  3. Neither $S_1$ nor $S_2$ is correct.
  4. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are correct

Match the pairs in the following question by choosing appropriate option.
$$\begin{array}{|c|cl|}\hline
P_1 & A&\text{There are exactly two mangoes}
\\\hline
P_2 &B&\text{There are at least two mangoes}
\\\hline
P_3 &C& \text{There is exactly one mango}
\\\hline
P_4 &D& \text{There are at least three mangoes}
\\\hline
\end{array}
$$
where,
$P_1:\exists x (\text{Mango}(x) \wedge \forall y (\text{Mango}(y) \implies y= x)) $
$P_2:\exists x \exists y(\text{Mango}(x) \wedge \text{Mango}(y) \wedge (x \ne y) \wedge \forall x \forall y \forall z ((\text{Mango}(x) \wedge \text{Mango}(y) \wedge \text{Mango}(z)) \implies (x=y \vee x=z \vee y=z)) $
$P_3:\exists x \exists y(\text{Mango}(x) \wedge \text{Mango}(y) \wedge (x \ne y) $
$P_4:\exists x \exists y \exists z(\text{Mango}(x) \wedge \text{Mango}(y) \wedge \text{Mango}(z)\wedge (x \ne y) \wedge (y \ne z) \wedge (x \ne z)$
 

  1. $P_1 - C, P_2 - A, P_3 - D, P_4 - B$
  2. $P_1 - C, P_2 - B, P_3 - D, P_4 - A$
  3. $P_1 - C, P_2 - A, P_3 - B, P_4 - D$
  4. None of the above

Consider the following logical statements:

  • $P_1:$ If it rained or one of the team did not turn up, the match would not be played.
  • $P_2:$ The match was played.

Which of the following is not a valid conclusion?

  1. It did not rain.
  2. It did not rain and no team turned up
  3. One team turned up
  4. All are valid conclusions

Which of the following is a valid partition for $N,$ where $N$ is the set of natural numbers? (Mark all the appropriate choices)

  1. $\{x \in N \mid x \geq 100 \} \cup \{x \in N \mid x \leq 100\}$
  2. $\{x \in N \mid x \geq 100 \} \cup \{x \in N \mid x < 100\}$
  3. $\{x \in N \mid x > 100 \} \cup \{x \in N \mid x < 100\}$
  4. $\{x \in N \mid x \geq 101 \} \cup \{x \in N \mid x < 100 \}$

Consider the following two statements about sets $X ,Y$ and $Z$
$S_1:$ If $X \subseteq Y$ and $Y \subseteq Z,$ then $X \subseteq Z.$
$S_2:$ If $X \in Y$ and $Y \in Z,$ then $X \in Z$
  1. Only $S_1$ is true
  2. Only $S_2$ is true
  3. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are true
  4. Neither $S_1$ nor $S_2$ is true

Which of the following is/are bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}?$ (Mark all the appropriate choices)

  1. $2x+1$
  2. $x^2+1$
  3. $x^3$
  4. $x$

Let $A,B$ and $C$ be three sets. Then $(A-B) - C$ is _________.

  1. $(A-B)-(B-C)$
  2. $(A-C)-(B-C)$
  3. $(B-C)-(A-C)$
  4. $(A-B)-(A-C)$

Consider the following function $f$ on $\left[-\frac{1}{2},3\right] \rightarrow [-1,1]$ such that $f(x) = \frac{2x-1}{4x+5}$. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. $f$ is not one-one but is onto
  2. $f$ is neither one-one nor onto
  3. $f$ is bijective
  4. $f$ is one-one but not onto

Given a relation $*$ on $Z^2$ by $(a,b)*(c,d)$ if and only if either $a<c$ or else $a=c$ and $b\leq d$. Consider the following statements.

  • $S_1:$ $*$ is transitive.
  • $S_2:$ $*$ is anti-symmetric.
  1. $S_1$ is TRUE and $S_2$ is FALSE
  2. $S_1$ is FALSE and $S_2$ is TRUE
  3. Neither $S_1$ nor $S_2$ is correct
  4. Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are correct.

Let $P(X)$ be the collection of all the subset of a set $X$ with at least three elements. Consider the following two relations on $P(X):$

  • $R:A \subseteq B$
  • $S: A \cap B = \phi$.

Which of the following is true about relations $R$ and $S?$

  1. $R$ is anti-symmetric but $S$ is not anti-symmetric.
  2. $R$ is not anti-symmetric but $S$ is anti-symmetric.
  3. Both $R$ and $S$ are anti-symmetric
  4. None of these

Consider set $A = \{\phi, \{1,2\},4,\{3\}\}.$ Which of the following is a subset of $A?$ (Mark all the appropriate choices)

  1. $\{1,2\}$
  2. $\{\{3\}\}$
  3. $\{3\}$
  4. $\{4,3\}$

The domain of the function $f$ defined by $f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x + |x|}}$ is.
  1. $\mathbb{R}$
  2. $\mathbb{R}^+$
  3. $\mathbb{R}- \{0\}$
  4. None of these

Let $a(t), b(t)$ and $c(t)$ be the lengths of three sides of a geometric figure $t$ in non-increasing order (i.e., $a(t) \geq b(t) \geq c(t)).$
We define the sets:

$\blacksquare X := \{t : a(t) = b(t)\}$
$\blacksquare Y := \{t : b(t) = c(t)\}$
$\blacksquare T := \{\text{the set of all triangles}\}$

Which of the following will represent an equilateral triangle?

  1. $(X \cup Y) \cap T$
  2. $X \cap Y \cap T$
  3. $X \oplus Y \oplus T$
  4. $X \cap Y$

Consider the following relations defined on set $I$:

  • $R_1:\{(x,y) \mid xy \geq 1 \}$
  • $R_2:\{(x,y) \mid x \equiv y(\mod 7) \}$
  • $R_3: \{(x,y) \mid x \neq y \}$

where $I$ is set of all non-negative integers. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. $R_1$ reflexive while $R_2$ and $R_3$ are not reflexive.
  2. $R_1$ and $R_3$ are not reflexive while $R_2$ is reflexive.
  3. $R_1,$ $R_2$ and $R_3$ are all reflexive.
  4. None of these relations is reflexive

$P$ and $Q$ are two prepositions. Which of the following logical expressions are equivalent?

  1. $\neg Q\rightarrow \neg P$
  2. $\neg P \vee Q$
  3. $P \rightarrow Q$
  4. $\neg P \wedge Q$
  1. I, IV
  2. I, II, III
  3. II, IV
  4. I, II, III, IV

Let's consider a propositional language where

  • $p$ means "$x$ is a power of $2$",
  • $q$ means "$x$ is even".

Which of the following is the correct formal representation of the sentence
"$x$ being a power of $2$ is a sufficient condition for $x$ being even"?

  1. $p \rightarrow q$
  2. $q \rightarrow p$
  3. $\neg p \rightarrow \neg q$
  4. none of these
